sections.heading: Chronology — read this before anything about "buildtime" and "runtime"
sections.text:
`[A 2026-09-15]` Early 2025: Hareet and Andra define the two tracks and their categories; the strategy is published in 2025 and implementation begins. Summer 2026: in a recorded Ground Truth conversation with Andra, Taylor Downs of OpenFn names the same split *buildtime AI* and *runtime AI*, with a sharper account of their differences, opportunity, and importance to stakeholders; Andra says on the recording that Medic already thought in two tracks. Hareet adopted the words because they explain the tracks better. **The tracks are Hareet's and Andra's; the words are Taylor's.** `[A-NOTES]` Taylor's argument: most real AI adoption in government systems happens at build time — cutting the cost of building secure, deterministic workflows — and that is the right first step. Andra's: build time is where model access is easy, while running a model on a two-gigabyte phone far from connectivity is the hard problem.
`[A 2026-10-29]` He keeps the words buildtime AI and runtime AI: he doesn't have to own the phrasing to be able to use the words, and he can give credit to a source that inspired him.

sections.heading: The strategy
sections.text:
**How it was made.** `[A 2026-09-14]` Hareet researched where other AI trials and pilots were aiming — mostly clinical decision support and chat support on the CHW side — then turned the tracks into the implementation ideas that mattered most to stakeholders, with supporting the CHW as the top priority. The strategy's "end-to-end, not just point-of-care" commitment is where that research landed.
**Two stories.** Grace, a CHW in Siaya County, Kenya, with more households than she can reach after the rains, choosing whom to visit from a list that doesn't know what she knows — in an app written in English, while she and the mothers she visits think in their own language. Pawan, a program manager in Nepal who knows exactly what a postpartum follow-up workflow should look like, but needs a developer, a specification process, and weeks of back-and-forth to get it built. The people closest to the problem have the knowledge; the technology doesn't meet them where they are. AI should close that gap without replacing their judgment.
**Seven questions it asks of AI entering community health** (paraphrased): Does it reach people offline, on low-cost devices? Is it shaped by the CHWs and program managers it serves? Is it owned by ministries rather than a vendor? Does it address what actually limits care, not only clinical decisions? Is it culturally and linguistically appropriate? Can a CHW understand why it recommended something? Does it reduce the burden, or add another app?
**AI-ready, not AI-first.** A distinction the strategy credits to Medic's Board Chair, Raffi Krikorian (CTO, Mozilla): chasing the newest models, versus having the foundation in place so AI does the work that matters. Fifteen years of building for the hardest environments produced a knowledge corpus of community health technology and a community of practice — governments, implementing partners, CHW networks, developers, researchers, and peer digital public goods — building on the same platform. The CHT community of practice spans 47+ organizations. Together, the community has equipped 182,000+ health workers. The community works across 24 countries. The community delivers care to an estimated 90 million people.
**The anchor and four commitments.** The anchor question above, then: *Access, not speed* — put capability, and with it power, in the hands of those who don't have it today. *Ownership, not dependency* — if a community can't run it, inspect it, modify it, or turn it off, it isn't built right. *End-to-end, not just point-of-care* — invest where real friction lives: scheduling, routing, supply prediction, supervision. *Build once, use everywhere* — the unglamorous shared infrastructure: sanitization tools, MCP servers, AI-ready data, packaged agent skills.
**Equity at the center.** Two questions — whose health improves (equity of outcomes) and who gets to build and to use (equity of access) — map to the two tracks. Augmenting the builder is how you augment the frontline at scale.
**Track 1 — inside the CHT: for health workers (runtime AI).** Statuses as the strategy states them.

sections.heading: The strategy
sections.text:
- *Smart Task Prioritization* — the CHT surfaces what matters most, from local data; identified by the community; active squad. `[A]` Hareet is its AI system architect; his pitch and design won the 2025 Momentum to Modernize award.
- *Route Optimization* — visits ordered by location, urgency, and real-world constraints; active squad.
- *Offline AI-Ready* — on-device inference, data layer first; emerging.
- *Local Language Coverage* — open models and language data for the languages CHWs actually use; emerging.
- *Voice Interfaces* — voice-to-text for visit notes, voice navigation for low-literacy users; exploring, dependent on language coverage. `[A 2026-09-27]` Voice for CHT, which Hareet designed, is the program here; its pilot is underway.
- *Supply Chain and Operational Intelligence* — stockout prediction, CHW dropout risk; emerging.
**Track 2 — around the CHT: for builders (buildtime AI).**
- *CHT Multi-Agent System* — platform-appropriate code and tests from plain-language descriptions, with human review at every step; the strategy targeted a proof of concept in the first half of 2026. `[A]` This is cht-agent, now in production for cht-conf. `[A 2026-10-28/29]` It is in production for cht-core too.
- *AI-Powered Interoperability* — the CHT connecting to other digital public goods faster; emerging.
- *CHT AI Tools* — shared infrastructure: data-sanitization scripts, MCP servers, reusable agent skills; the codebase and documentation MCP servers were already live when it was written. `[A]` Hareet built both MCP servers.
- *AI for Non-Technical Configuration* — forms, dashboards, and translations without code; emerging. `[A]` This is No-Code CHT Configuration; Hareet is its AI system architect.

sections.heading: The strategy
sections.text:
- `[A 2026-09-14]` Buildtime AI in Hareet's words: taking dreams that would have cost massive engineering time off the shelf — after first building the harnesses and skills that let AI build them reliably — and changing cht-core's development lifecycle by using cht-agent, guided so non-technical users can drive it.
**How we build.** Organizational AI, not individual AI: shared tools, standards, and learning. Foundation before features. Open-source models and tools, with commercial APIs for prototyping and always an exit door. Human-in-the-loop, always — CHWs often perceive AI as infallible, so the design works against that assumption. Consolidated intelligence, not more apps: every capability lives inside the CHT.
**Partnerships.** Every AI project runs through a multi-organization squad. Medic learns from partners ahead of it (Audere, D-tree, Dalberg, and others); holds research partnerships with the University of British Columbia (SmartDischarges), Berkeley (ChatCHW), Strathmore University (an adolescent health chatbot), ComBaCal, and Tanuh.ai; engages funders; and seeks language and voice partnerships with open-source language-model communities, academic NLP groups working on low-resource languages, and ministries leading national language digitization.
**Roadmap — the plan as published, not delivery claims.** Live at publication: the CHT documentation and codebase MCP servers, a Kapa.ai documentation assistant, and two partner pilots at the point of care — AI-assisted malaria RDT reading with HealthPulseAI (Uganda and Kenya) and oral cancer screening with Tanuh.AI. Create: the multi-agent system (Q2 2026) and a public collection of CHT AI tools (Q3 2026). Design: a CHT architecture revamp (Q3 2026), smart task prioritization with route optimization (Q3 2026), non-technical configuration (Q4 2026). Explore: offline on-device models (Q4 2026), AI for interoperability (Q3 2026), local language coverage (Q4 2026), voice interfaces (Q1 2027).

sections.heading: agent-watchdog — the newest agent in production
sections.text:
- `[A 2026-09-27]` Built by Hareet and released to production; the newest agent Medic runs.
- `[C]` What it does (public README: github.com/medic/cht-ai-tools, `packages/agent-watchdog`): a daily analysis of the CHT projects monitored by Medic's hosted CHT Watchdog, posted to Slack as a short brief that flags what a human should look into. It reads metrics through Grafana, computes changes deterministically, and gives a bounded Claude Agent SDK session read-only tools to interpret them; every number, date, and link is verified in code before anything posts. Reactions and thread notes shape the next day's brief; what the agent learns arrives as proposal files for human review, never as changes to its own prompts, skills, or thresholds. It flags and never acts; paging stays with the existing monitoring stack.
- `[A 2026-09-27]` It saves patterns, projects, and user feedback, and posts daily to Slack or another configured channel.
- `[C]` How it's built: spec-first, with its own Spec Kit constitution and specs and an `AGENTS.md`; a staged pipeline (purge, feedback, collect, analyze, agent, rollup, render, publish) that can run one stage at a time, dry-run without posting, or replay stored runs against changed prompts; weekly threshold calibration; a hardened container (non-root, read-only root filesystem, no capabilities), an offline profile, and a command that lists every destination a run contacts.

sections.heading: Voice for CHT — Track 1's voice program
sections.text:
The brief calls it Voice for CHT; Hareet also calls it voice-to-CHT.
- **The idea.** Speak the visit; the form fills itself. As the CHW talks, values land in the form — a child's age, how long a fever has lasted, a weight — and anything implausible is flagged to check. The CHW confirms, then saves.
- **Why.** CHWs spend much of every visit reading and typing forms, often in English — a second or third language. Voice in their own language hands the typing to the app and gives that time back to care.
- **Why now.** An offline speech model for the pilot language already exists, built by a speech-model partner for the resource-constrained phones CHWs carry. It needs tuning to CHW vocabulary, which it learns from recordings without anyone transcribing them.
- **The pilot.** One workflow, one language, a small cohort at one or two facilities. Four stages, each gated by the one before rather than by dates: CHWs record consented visits during normal work (20–30 hours in all); the partner tunes the model on those voices while Medic builds form-filling into the CHT; a supervised field test against pass/fail criteria agreed first; then findings and documentation go to the CHT community as a protocol any partner can repeat in its own language. Beyond the pilot: CHT-to-voice, with synced reports read back to CHWs in their language.
- **Who does what.** `[A 2026-09-27]` Hareet designed the idea, the project, and the capability; went looking for a partner who already had some of Medic's languages working in small models, and found one; and built Medic's side. `[A-DOC brief]` The speech-model partner: the offline speech models. Medic: the CHT platform and integration. A CHW partner organization: CHWs, voices, and feedback. `[A 2026-09-14]` The program is the strategy's runtime-AI answer to its top priority, supporting the CHW. `[A 2026-09-02/14]` It won credits.

sections.heading: Voice for CHT — Track 1's voice program
sections.text:
- `[A 2026-10-28/29]` He designed the idea, found the team, helped them fine-tune models to 273 MB so they run beside the app on a rural health worker's 4 GB Android phone, and built Medic's side. The hardware specs illustrate the impact of fine-tuning models for offline low-resource phones.
- **Honest by design.** Open source, permanently — device model weights under Apache-2.0, models fine-tuned on community audio stay open, and the CHT stays open. The community owns its data — contributors choose the licence; transcripts are stripped of personal health information before any downstream system; recordings are held under the consent agreement contributors sign. CHWs are protected — review before submit, always; no audio or transcript leaves the phone as telemetry; a CHW's data never evaluates that CHW; opting out carries no consequence. Measured honestly — success criteria agreed in writing before the pilot; results published with failures included, every number with its method.
- **What isn't known yet.** How accuracy holds up on real clinic audio (a dip is expected, then gains); who said what in multi-speaker visits; how numbers, dosages, and IDs perform, and whether the errors that slip through are ones a CHW can catch in review rather than plausible wrong values; whole-visit versus guided field-by-field capture; what the slowest handsets run well.
- **Status.** `[A 2026-09-27]` The pilot is underway. Field results come later, published by the brief's own rules.
- **Next.** `[A 2026-09-27]` Medic plans to build its own in-house voice-to-CHT for Nepali and rural Nepali dialects — a plan, not work done.

sections.heading: Snowboarding
sections.text:
- `[A 2026-11-06]` How it started, in his words: "I moved to Colorado about 15 years ago, and met my now-wife here, who had recently moved back to her hometown. We spent 10 years traveling through Sub-Saharan Africa and Asia setting up work projects, which I'll tell you about related to Medic. Whenever we arrived back home, we always fell in love with our state of Colorado, the most gorgeous state in the Union. More recently, we decided to take up Winter Sports and got back into Snowboarding. With the help of a neighbor, he was able to provide me with all the necessary gear to get going. We live in a city house in Denver, so I throw on a snowboard bag and ride a bicycle to the train station where I can board with all my equipment and be dropped directly off at Winter Park Resort and ski lifts. It's a great experience and I think the only resort in North America accessible via train. You can often find me there, snowboarding through the trees, enjoying the back side of the mountain. We hope to gear up and travel for a destination snowboard trip soon, eagerly awaiting a chance to snowboard in Japan. If you are local to Colorado, we are Ikon Pass people, simply due to the better public transit offerings to their mountains."
- `[A 2026-11-06]` When he first learned, in his words: "As a child, but I never took lessons or had the proper clothing, so I never enjoyed it or got beyond the very basics. Recently, as an adult, I decided to self-teach myself with YouTube and iteration. Now I'm successfully going down double black diamond slopes."
- `[A 2026-11-06]` What he loves most about it now, in his words: "Enjoying riding through the trees on a fresh snowy day."

sections.heading: Biking
sections.text:
- `[A 2026-11-06]` The riding he does, in his words: "Commuter riding around the city. I ride to my parents' house to have lunch weekly, I also ride a one-wheel and love exploring the extended city neighborhoods on a bicycle."
- `[A 2026-11-06]` What he loves about getting around the city by bike, in his words: "The weather is usually sunny and gorgeous, and biking allows you to take more of the outside in. I don't like driving at all, and only drive if I'm going hiking in the mountains and taking my dog. I even enjoy winter biking and layering up in clothes to keep warm and enjoying the crisp air."

sections.heading: Arya
sections.text: - `[A 2026-11-06]` His dog, in his words: "Arya is a Nova Scotia Duck Tolling Retriever, known as a Duck Toller. When I used to stay in Minneapolis, one of my colleagues invited me up to a cabin at Lake of the Woods, which is a State Park at the border of Minnesota and Canada. My first time going up to a cabin, I thought we were camping outside in the cold and brought a ton of appropriate equipment. Instead, the cabin was essentially a second home, full of furnishings, isolated deep in Lake of the Woods. One of the neighbors during that stay was on a hunting trip, and had 3 duck tollers with him. I ended up playing with the dogs for the entire time we were there, that my friend offered me the keys to the cabin and told me I should come back and grab a dog or puppy from the neighbor. Within weeks, I had brought Arya back home and my life forever changed. She has kept me outside, active, walking, and playing when most of my hobbies and work life revolved around computers or tinkering with hardware. She introduced me to most of my friends, and especially my wife. Arya is now 13 years old, and has went camping across the country and across Canada several times with me. She's always up for an adventure, but certainly enjoys a snooze in her senior years. <3"

sections.heading: Travel
sections.text:
- `[A 2026-11-06]` The trip that has stayed with him most, in his words: "Traveling for work has elevated the relationships, connections, and my love for the places visited to another degree. Most recently, I was in Senegal to visit my CEO and discuss our plan for offline voice-to-CHT models, as I was traveling to Nigeria afterwards to discuss with the partner on our implementation. In Lagos, I also visited Fela Kuti's Shrine and got to see local music at the same sites that Wizkid, Burna Boy and others grew up and made famous. The hospitality, friendliness, energy, and AI-for-good projects, will always have a place in my heart."
- `[A 2026-11-06]` What all those years of traveling for work taught him, in his words: "That's tough to answer. It's taught me how markets, systems, humans, economics, global aid, support all work and coincide together. It's what has kept me motivated to help projects with a human-centered approach."
- The work projects from those years are in `06-work-projects.md`.

sections.text:

Similar to work I do for Medic, finding a team mission and showing up for those around you who share that goal is unifying experience for me."

sections.heading: When new technology is worth it
sections.text:
- `[A 2026-11-06]` In his words: "Taking into consideration the effectiveness of using deterministic approaches, and how cost effective the evaluation, resource-usage, and maintenance is on AI solutions. For example, at Medic, our Community Health Workers, had older Android phones with roughly 2-4GB [of RAM] on them, and were mainly without network access. Building the application to be reliant on larger models that were unable to run on their phone was effectively a non-starter. I spent time architecting AI solutions that could run on their phones, which we labeled as Runtime AI in our Medic AI strategy that I co-authored with our CEO. This included fine-tuning offline local language voice models to fill out CHT forms."
- `[A 2026-11-06]` Smart Task Prioritization's design, in his words: "This was architected in a manner that once a week, if network access was available, the client would synchronize tasks with a deeper reasoning and higher context model, and on the local offline device it ran a small ML on an existing priority score configuration."
- `[A 2026-11-06]` Buildtime AI, in his words: "A different focus around AI in our strategy was Buildtime AI, and my focus was to pull engineering dreams off the shelf, that were once unattainable or too time consuming, and detail out the implementation path towards them. For Medic, this meant allowing non-technical users the ability to participate in the creation of new features and maintainability of the software. I architected and built the cht-agent, a multi-agent you can deploy, install with all the considerations an SRE brings: cost-effectiveness, model agnostic, locally-owned, context management, curated domain knowledge-corpus."

sections.heading: Two lanes
sections.text:
- `[A-DOC site]` Every document goes down one of two lanes, and a written rule picks the lane. Local AI keeps sensitive data on hardware the client owns or leases, in their office or their own data center. Cloud AI improves fastest and is good for research, drafting, and ideas.
- `[A-DOC site]` Before anything can go to cloud AI, cleaning software swaps names, account numbers, and other identifiers for tags. Every cloud request shows the cleaned text that went out, so staff and owners can check it.
- `[A 2026-11-06]` What happens to anything bound for cloud AI, in his words: "Anything bound for Cloud AI is pre and post processed by custom software we create alongside your team that ensures no sensitive material ever touches Cloud AI".

- `[A-DOC site]` The client's team writes the rules with Denver Local AI. Anything from a tax return takes the local lane even after cleaning, and so does a law office's matter file unless the client consents.
- `[A-DOC site]` What the client owns: the software and the written rules ("They're yours, not a subscription."); a test report (identifiers planted in sample files, how many the cleaning caught, and every miss listed); a "What leaves your office" sheet for their security plan; and the freedom to switch AI companies, because the software works with any model.

sections.heading: How they work
sections.text:
1. `[A-DOC site]` Learn the tasks: which chores eat staff time, which files they touch, and how the team uses AI today, including personal ChatGPT accounts.
2. `[A-DOC site]` Clean up the files: de-duplicate folders and records, then build the cleaning software, tested on the client's own documents with every miss listed.
3. `[A-DOC site]` Set up private AI on the client's own hardware: a local model on a computer in the office, a server behind their VPN, or their own data center, with no per-use fees. Depending on the hardware, it can run with the internet switched off.
4. `[A-DOC site]` Build the pathways with the team: for each task, a written rule and the software that follows it (local or cloud AI, which tool, and what gets cleaned first), and an AI section for their security plan.
5. `[A-DOC site]` Train the team and stay close: staff practise with their own questions, then a weekly visit and regular catch-ups, with the rules updated when the tools change.
